01-feature-building.notes: All 23 pass the 5 hidden contract tests and their own suites, so the ranking comes from my probes: duplicate dependency entries, 10k-node cycles, scale, and cycle message precision. It also uses a mutation run of each suite against 18 mutants of a reference implementation. Contract deductions: A (duplicate-dependency bug, sometimes returning duplicated IDs), D/H/T (RecursionError on cycles longer than about 1,000 jobs), N/R (reject whitespace-only IDs). Cycle messages that list downstream jobs (B, E, F, J, P, Q, V, W) lose 0.25, since the brief only asks for IDs 'when practical'. Closest calls: C vs K (both perfect; C first on its slightly cleaner single-cycle diagnostic), and L vs the S/M/G/O cluster. O lost 0.5 on tests for its self-reported fuzzing outside the task directory, which is not recorded in any process_note. Some mutant survivals were masked because those suites assert their own message wording and fail on my reference too. I spot-checked N by hand: its cycle and ID tests still fail the mutants with 'ScheduleError not raised'. Not verified: the Python versions quoted in RESPONSE files. The non-Job, unhashable-dependency and depends_on=None behaviours fall outside the written contract and served only as tie-breaks.

02-bug-fixing.notes: All 23 implementations matched a reference model on get() outcomes across 3000 random sequences, and all handle validation and the injected clock correctly. Behaviour differs only in expired-entry retention: G and W never delete on an expired get (hidden test failure), and R purges only when full. Regression coverage was scored mainly from a mutation matrix: 17 contract-level mutants of a reference fix (falsy check, wall clock, > boundary, no LRU on get, get refreshes TTL, update without recency/timestamp/value, evict-on-update, no purge, purge only from the LRU front, purge after evicting, evict MRU, weakened validations), plus one non-contract mutant (expired get keeps entry). The most common blind spots were tests that place the expired entry at the LRU end (so no purge still passes) and update tests that update the LRU key (so evict-then-assign still passes). Over-specified len tests (A, D, U) were docked 0.25 because they reject valid implementations. C/O's below-capacity purge test was not docked, since the contract can be read as always purging. The six 10.0 scores are ordered by mutant kills, including the non-contract one (F, P, J, O kill all 18; C and M miss it), then by documented verification. D and F mention copies of the original outside the task directory; no process_note was recorded for them, and I did not deduct. I could not verify reported timings or Python versions.

06-product-planning.notes: Grading was done by reading every PLAN.md and RESPONSE.md in full and checking each against BRIEF.md/TASK.md. OBJECTIVE_CHECKS.json was empty ({} per letter) and no process_note was present. There is nothing executable to run for this planning task. Mechanical checks: word counts (about 2.4k-11k words per plan), a grep for dates/durations/headcounts (hits in K: 'Week 1/2/3 post-pilot'; O: '1 week/2 weeks/4 weeks', '2 days'; I: '2-3 Weeks', '2-week'; E, H and V: invented cohort sizes and durations), and confirmation that BRIEF.md/TASK.md in each folder match the originals. The main differentiator was the 24h purge versus an offline device: F (Layer 2 cap anchored on server submission time), D/M/S (purge on confirmed submission), B/U/W (acceptance gated on purge receipts) and L (accept = submit commit) close the gap. A/G/P/Q/T/V/N/K/I rely on the device learning of acceptance, and G/P explicitly weaken the deadline. The second differentiator was the conflict policy: timestamp LWW (C, N), server-wins that drops inspector notes (R, V, O) and aggregate-only conflicts (U, W, B) were judged against preserve-and-review approaches. Close calls: F vs D/S. F edges ahead on explicit proof of the purge bound, clock anchoring and traceability; D vs S is near-equal, and D is ranked first for its field-class ownership and orphaned-work handling. 13-frontend-playful.notes: F vs J vs A was the closest call. All three are expressive, complete and keyboard-friendly. F wins on its distinctive shape language and its three-zone desktop; J's sticky detail with an observation field is equally complete but costs a little on implementation (localStorage persistence); A's two-column desktop leaves more dead space. R/D/T/P/U form the next tier, ordered by taste and layout. Generic heuristics mislabelled some first-try clicks (B/H/L/P/U card buttons), so undo-after-done for those was confirmed in follow-up runs and screenshots. C and Q are functionally broken: C's [hidden] override leaves an undismissable modal; Q has an undefined label and empty bars. Contrast figures come from a rough walk-up-the-ancestors background estimate and are indicative only. I did not use a screen reader.
